newsitem.title: UK: Britain to go ahead with selective cattle cull.
newsitem.headline: Britain to go ahead with selective cattle cull.

text.p: Britain said on Monday it would go ahead with a selective cull of cattle in a bid to persuade the European Union to lift the ban on the export of British beef it imposed because of mad cow disease.

"We have decided that now is the time to bring forward our proposals for a selective cull in accordance with the terms of the Florence agreement..." British farm minister Douglas Hogg told Parliament.
A selective cull was agreed by Prime Minister John Major with other EU heads of government at the Florence summit last June, as part of a package to end the crisis over mad cow disease.

But Hogg said he could not be certain how many cattle would now need to be slaughtered under the selective cull, which would come on top of the one million cattle already slain in Britain in response to the mad cow scare.
He said the government's original estimate of 128,000 cattle was out of date, as many of these animals would have been slaughtered already.
He added: "If for example we were required to deal with around 100,000 animals, the gross net cost would be around 150 million pounds and the net cost around 90 million pounds.
"The difference is contributions from EU funds and the OTMS (over 30 months scheme)," Hogg said.
